ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (neuromuscular) Consultation — Dorothea Lange — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Diagnosis of post-polio syndrome with the neuromuscular rehabilitation consultation the same day; bone density and spirometry

text.paragraph: New fatigue, slowly increasing weakness in the left leg and both arms as well as the right leg weakened by paralytic polio at seven, muscle aching after work, and two falls, over about 18 months, in a photographer of 61. Is this post-polio syndrome, and how should she be managed so that she can keep working? [S]

list.item: Does she meet the criteria for post-polio syndrome, and have other causes of new weakness been excluded?
How should exercise be prescribed so that it helps without overusing weakened muscles?
Which orthosis and walking aid would prevent falls and still let her work in the field?
Does she need respiratory or sleep studies?
What precautions should be recorded for sedation and anesthesia, since she may need an endoscopy?
How should she pace her work, and what can she expect over the coming years?

text.paragraph: Ms. Lange is seen at the request of Dr. Ashford-Mensah. She had polio at seven, with weakness of the right leg from which she partly recovered; she walked without an aid for more than 50 years and worked long days on her feet carrying cameras. Over about 18 months she has developed fatigue after two hours of activity, weakness of the left thigh and both shoulders, increased weakness of the right leg, aching after work, cold intolerance of the right foot, and two falls from catching the right foot. She has no sensory symptoms, swallowing trouble, breathlessness, or morning headaches; her sleep is unrefreshing. She asked for a plain answer about whether she would have to stop working. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Dorothea Lange was born Dorothea Margaretta Nutzhorn in Hoboken, New Jersey, on May 26, 1895. [D]
At the age of seven, in 1902, Lange had polio, which left her with a weakened right leg and a lifelong limp. [D]

Lange was a documentary photographer. In 1935 she was hired as a photographer for the Resettlement Administration, later the Farm Security Administration, and in March 1936 she made the photograph known as "Migrant Mother" in Nipomo, California. From the mid-1930s she lived in Berkeley, California. [D]
In the late 1940s ill health stopped Lange working: she had a succession of severe stomach ulcers that were controlled only by radical surgery, and pain and discomfort troubled her from then on. [D]
In the early 1950s Lange returned to work with photographic essays for Life and Fortune and helped to found the photography magazine Aperture; her poor health limited her to short bursts of work. [D]

list.item: Post-polio syndrome (G14). She meets the modified March of Dimes criteria. Prior paralytic polio is confirmed by history, examination, and EMG, which shows chronic reinnervation in the right leg and, more mildly, in the left vastus lateralis and right deltoid, so polio affected more muscles than she knew. Partial recovery was followed by decades of stable function, and the new weakness and fatigue have lasted more than a year. Normal nerve conduction excludes neuropathy and entrapment, the EMG shows no myopathy and no decrement on repetitive stimulation, and the blood tests exclude thyroid disease, anemia, diabetes, B12 deficiency, and inflammation; the mildly raised creatine kinase fits overuse. Depression is mild and secondary. No drug has a proven effect on post-polio syndrome, so pyridostigmine, amantadine, and corticosteroids are not recommended. [S]

Exercise. Supervised, individualized training at submaximal effort improves strength, fatigue, and pain without harming motor units if it does not cause exhaustion or aching the next day. Warm-water exercise suits her cold intolerance. [S]

Orthosis and falls. Both falls come from right foot drop, and the knee hyperextension strains the knee. A custom lightweight carbon-fiber ankle-foot orthosis will clear the foot and control the knee, and is light enough to wear on field days; a cane in the left hand unloads the right leg. A knee-ankle-foot orthosis is not needed now because the knee does not buckle. [S]

Respiratory and sleep. No breathlessness or bulbar symptoms, a normal cough, and normal spirometry today make respiratory muscle weakness unlikely. Unrefreshing sleep should be screened with home overnight oximetry; sleep apnea and nocturnal hypoventilation are more common in polio survivors. [S]

Sedation and anesthesia. Polio survivors can be sensitive to sedatives, opioids, and neuromuscular blocking drugs and may have unrecognized respiratory weakness, cold intolerance, and positioning problems. For an endoscopy, moderate sedation at reduced doses with oxygen and carbon dioxide monitoring is appropriate. [S]

Pacing and outlook. Post-polio syndrome usually progresses slowly, over years, and pacing, the right exercise, and an orthosis often stabilize function or improve it. She can keep working in the field with planned rest and less to carry. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Ashford-Mensah's referral and examination; blood tests from the first visit (hemoglobin 13.1, TSH 2.1, HbA1c 5.4 percent, B12 512, creatinine 0.7, ESR 12, CRP 0.3, creatine kinase 228, 25-hydroxyvitamin D 22); nerve conduction studies and needle EMG performed in this department a week ago; spirometry and the bone density scan done today. [S]

list.item: Twelve weeks of supervised physical therapy, twice a week: submaximal strengthening with rest days, aerobic and warm-water exercise, gait and balance training, and energy conservation; then a home program. Stop any exercise that leaves her exhausted or aching the next day. [S]
Custom lightweight carbon-fiber right ankle-foot orthosis, fitted within four weeks, and a single-point cane in the left hand. [S]
Pacing for field days: a lighter camera on a harness, a seat stick, an assistant to carry the tripod, rest breaks every hour, and a rest day after each field day. [S]
Baseline spirometry today, then yearly or with symptoms; home overnight oximetry for unrefreshing sleep. [S]

Record sedation and anesthesia precautions in the chart: reduced sedative and opioid doses, continuous oxygen and carbon dioxide monitoring, warming, careful positioning of the right leg, and caution with neuromuscular blocking drugs. [S]
No disease-specific drug; acetaminophen, heat, and pacing for pain; no NSAIDs after her ulcer surgery. [S]

Bone density of both hips and the spine, since disuse of the right leg and falls raise fracture risk; the scan done today by primary care shows osteoporosis of the right hip, which primary care will treat. [S]
Review in this clinic at six months, or sooner for new weakness, breathlessness, or swallowing trouble. [S]
Discussed with Dr. Ashford-Mensah the same day; Ms. Lange has a written summary of the diagnosis, the exercise and pacing plan, and the sedation precautions, and agreed to the plan. [S]
Follow-up: Physical therapy and orthotics will start the program; this clinic reviews her at six months. Primary care coordinates the bone density result, the oximetry, and any endoscopy. [S]
